terms.comment: Anyone working for pay (mercēs); a woman is mercēnāria (Traupman 309). Also written mercēnnārius (de Vaan 376: mercēn(n)ārius). Cicero counts wage-labour among the meaner livelihoods (Off. 1.150), so the word can sound low; for an office worker see minister.
Classically a servant or attendant (Lewis & Short); Levi and Bini give it for an employee, with the periphrasis quī operam mercēde dat, one who works for pay.

phrases.latin: Est autem īnfima condiciō et fortūna servōrum, quibus nōn male praecipiunt quī ita jubent ūtī, ut mercēnnāriīs, operam exigendam, jūsta praebenda.
phrases.english: The lowest condition and lot is that of slaves, and those who tell us to treat them like hired workers give good advice: demand the work, give them what is fair.
